source_text: Ἔνθα τοσοῦτόν τισι τῶν θερ μοτέρων ἐδυσχεράναμεν, ὥστε ἀπεπήδησαν ἡμῶν, τὸ φίλτρον εἰς ἔχθραν τρέψαντες. Οὐ γὰρ ἐξ ὧν χαριούμεθα σκοποῦμεν μᾶλλον, ἢ ἐξ ὧν ὠφε λήσομεν. Γʹ. Τίς οὖν ἡ αἰτία τοῦ τοσούτου περὶ ἡμᾶς πό θου, καὶ τοὺς λόγους τοὺς ἡμετέρους, αὐτοὶ βούλεσθε δηλῶσαι ταύτην καὶ παραστῆσαι, καὶ τὸ ὑμέτερον πάθος αὐτοὶ γνωρίσαι, ἢ δι' ἡμῶν τοῦτο δημοσιεῦσαι, ὡς καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἡμῖν χρῆσθε προθύμως ἐξηγηταῖς; Ἡμέτερον οἶδ' ὅτι ποιεῖσθε τὸν λόγον, ὅσον ἐκ τῆς ἡσυχίας τεκμαίρομαι. Οὐκοῦν ἀκούσατε, καὶ σκοπεῖτε, μὴ φαῦλος ἐγὼ τῶν τοιούτων εἰκαστής. Ἐμοὶ δοκεῖτε μάλιστα μὲν, ὡς αὐτοὶ καλέσαντες ἡμᾶς, οἰκείᾳ βοηθεῖν κρίσει, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο περιέπειν τὸ ὑμέτερον θήραμα. Φύσις δὲ αὕτη πρὸς τὸ οἰκεῖον ἅπαν εὐμενῶς ἔχειν, εἴτε κτῆμα, εἴτε γέννημα, εἴτε λόγον, καὶ δι' εὐνοίας ἑκουσίου χειροῦσθαι τοῖς ἑαυ τῶν προβλήμασιν. Δεύτερον δὲ, οὐδὲν οὕτως αἰ δεῖσθαι, ὡς τὸ μὴ ἰταμὸν ἡμῶν, μήτε βίαιον, μήτε θεατρικόν τε καὶ πανηγυρικὸν, ἀλλ' ὑποχωρη τικόν τε καὶ μέτριον, καὶ οἷον ἄκοινον ἐν τῷ κοινῷ, καὶ μονότροπον, καὶ, συντομώτερον εἰπεῖν ἔτι, φιλόσοφον· οὐδὲ αὐτὸ τεχνικῶς, καὶ πολιτικῶς ἡμῖν ἀνευρημένον, ἀλλ' ἁπλῶς καὶ πνευματικῶς τετιμημένον. Οὐ γὰρ, ἵνα ζητηθῶμεν, ἀποκρυπτόμεθα, οὐδ' ἵνα πλείονος ἄξιοι δόξωμεν τιμῆς, ὥσπερ οἱ τὰς ὥρας μικρὸν προφαίνοντες, εἶθ' ὑποστέλλοντες· ἀλλ' ἵνα τὸ φεύγειν τὰς προεδρίας, καὶ μὴ μεταποιεῖσθαι τῶν τοιούτων τιμῶν, τῷ ἡσυχίῳ δείξω μεν. Τρίτον, ὁρῶντες ἡμᾶς οἷα πάσχομεν ὑπό τε τῶν ἔξωθεν πολεμούντων, καὶ τῶν ἔνδοθεν ἐπιβουλευόντων· ἐπειδὴ, κατὰ τὸν Δανιὴλ, ἐξῆλθεν ἀνομία ἐκ πρεσβυτέρων ἐκ Βαβυλῶνος, οἳ ἐδόκουν κρί νειν τὸν Ἰσραήλ· σχετλιάζειν μὲν καὶ δυσχεραίνειν, καὶ οὐκ ἔχειν ὅπως ἐπαμύνητε τυραννουμένῳ, μό νον δὲ ἀντὶ πάντων εἰσφέρειν τὸν ἔλεον. Ὁ οὖν οἶκτος τῇ αἰδοῖ συγκραθεὶς φίλτρον ἐγένετο. Καὶ τοῦτο τῆς περὶ ἐμὲ τιμῆς τὸ μυστήριον. Δʹ. Ἐπεὶ δὲ οἱ λόγοι τὸ πολεμούμενον, καὶ ἡ περιττὴ καὶ ἐπίφθονος αὕτη γλῶττα, ἣν ἐν τοῖς ἔξωθεν παιδευθεῖσαν λόγοις, τοῖς θείοις ἐξευγενίσαμεν, καὶ τὴν πικρὰν καὶ ἄποτον Μεῤῥὰν τῷ τῆς ζωῆς ξύλῳ κατεγλυκάναμεν, πεπόνθατέ τι πάθος ἱκανῶς ἐλευθέριον· τοῦτο στέργετε, δι' ὃ πολεμούμεθα. Τί γὰρ οὐ τὴν κωφὴν ἠσπασάμεθα παίδευσιν; τί δὲ οὐ τὴν ξηράν τε καὶ κάτω βαίνουσαν; τί δαὶ ταύτῃ χαίροντας τοὺς πολλοὺς ὁρῶντες, ἐφιλοσοφοῦμεν ξένα καὶ ἔκφυλα, καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἀντιθέτους γλώσσας ἱστάμεθα; δέον θρασύτητι φεύγειν τοὺς λογισμοὺς, καὶ πίστιν ὀνομάζειν τὴν ἀλογίαν, ἣν ἠγάπησα ἂν καὶ αὐ τὸς, εὖ ἴστε, ἁλιεὺς ὤν· ἐπειδὴ τοῦτο πρόχειρον τοῖς πολλοῖς εἰς ἀπολογίαν τῆς ἀμαθίας· εἰ λόγον εἶχον τῶν σημείων τὴν δύναμιν. Ὡς ἀπόλοιτο ἐξ ἀνθρώ πων ὁ φθόνος, ἡ δαπάνη τῶν ἐχόντων, ὁ τῶν πα σχόντων ἰὸς, τὸ μόνον τῶν παθῶν ἀδικώτανόν τε ἅμα καὶ δικαιότατον· τὸ μὲν, ὅτι πᾶσι διοχλεῖ τοῖς καλοῖς· τὸ δὲ, ὅτι τήκει τοὺς ἔχοντας. Οὐ γὰρ τοῖς πρώτως ἐπαινέσασιν ἡμᾶς καταράσομαι· οὐ γὰρ ᾔδεισαν τῶν ἐπαίνων τὸ τέλος· ὡς τάχα ἄν τι καὶ λοιδορίας προσέθηκαν, ἵνα τὸν φθόνον ἐπίσχωσιν.
thought_title: Why the people love him and his words
orientation: Gregory is speaking to the people in Constantinople to explain the cause of their longing for him and his words as their support for their own choice, his retiring manner, and their pity for his suffering.
pass_a_gloss: There we displeased some of the more fervent so greatly that they sprang away from us, having turned affection into hatred. For we aim not rather from things by which we will please than from things by which we will benefit. 3. What then is the cause of such longing concerning us and our words, do you yourselves wish to make this clear and to exhibit it, and to make known your own feeling yourselves, or to publish this through us, as you also readily use us as interpreters of other things? I know you make the speech mine, as much as I conjecture from the silence. Listen therefore, and consider whether I am a worthless guesser of such things. To me you seem most of all, as having invited us yourselves, to assist your own judgment, and for this reason to cherish your own prey. For this is nature to be kindly disposed toward everything that is one's own, whether possession or offspring or speech, and to be mastered by one's own proposals through willing goodwill. Second, to revere nothing so much as our lack of shamelessness, nor violence, nor theatrical and festal manner, but retiring and moderate, and as it were uncommon in the public place, and solitary in manner, and, to say still more briefly, belonging to philosophical life; itself not devised by us artfully and politically, but honored simply and spiritually. For we do not hide ourselves in order that we may be sought, nor in order that we may seem worthy of greater honor, as those who show the seasons a little then draw them back; but in order that we may show by quietness the fleeing from front seats and the not laying claim to such honors. Third, seeing what things we suffer both from those outside warring and from those inside plotting; since, according to Daniel, lawlessness came forth from elders from Babylon, who seemed to judge Israel; to lament and to be displeased, and not to have how you might aid one tyrannized over, but only to bring in pity instead of all things. The pity therefore mixed together with shame became affection. And this is the mystery of the honor concerning me. 4. But since the words are the thing warred against, and this excessive and envied tongue, which having been trained in the teachings from outside we ennobled by the divine teachings, and we made sweet the bitter and undrinkable Marah by the wood of life, you have suffered a sufficiently noble suffering; this you love, on account of which we are warred against. For why did we not embrace the deaf education? Why not the dry and downward walking? Why then seeing the many rejoicing in this, did we philosophize strange and outgrown things, and stand against the opposing tongues? when we ought by boldness to flee reasonings, and to call unreason faith, which I myself would have loved, know well, being a fisherman; since this is ready at hand for the many as defense of ignorance; if I had the power of signs instead of speech. May envy perish from among humans, the expense of those having it, the poison of those suffering it, the only one of passions at once most unjust and most just; the one, because it troubles all good things; the other, because it melts those having it. For I will not curse those who first praised us; for they did not know the end of the praises; so that perhaps they would have added even something of reviling, in order that they might check envy.

pass_b_english: There I offended some of the hotter spirits so deeply that they broke away from me, turning their affection into hatred. I aim, you see, not so much at what will please people as at what will do them good.

What then is the reason for this great longing for me and for my preaching? Do you want to state and set it out yourselves, and explain your own feeling, or shall I publish it through my own lips, since you gladly use me to interpret so much else? I know you are giving the speech to me, as I judge from your silence. So listen, and judge whether I am a poor guesser at such things. First, I think, because you invited me yourselves, you are standing by your own judgment, and for that reason you cherish your own prey. It is human nature to look kindly on anything of our own, whether a possession or a child or an argument, and with willing favor to be won over by our own choices.

Second, you honor nothing in me so much as this, that I am not brazen or violent or theatrical and showy, but retiring and measured, almost a stranger in public life, solitary in manner, and, to put it most briefly, belonging to the philosophical life. And even that life I have not contrived with craft or calculation, but I honor it simply and spiritually. I do not hide myself to make people seek me, nor to seem worthy of greater honor, like those who show themselves for a moment and then withdraw. I do it to show by my quiet that I am fleeing the front seats and laying no claim to such honors.

Third, you see what I suffer from enemies attacking me outside and plotters scheming inside, since, as Daniel says, “Lawlessness came forth from elders in Babylon who seemed to judge Israel” (Susanna 5). You grieve and are indignant, and since you have no other way to help a man under tyranny, you offer the one gift that stands for all the rest, your pity. So pity mixed with respect has become affection. That is the secret of the honor you show me.

My preaching is the thing under attack, along with this fluent and envied tongue, which was trained in secular learning and which I have ennobled with divine truth. I have made bitter and undrinkable Marah sweet with the wood of life (Exodus 15:23), and you have felt something nobly generous in response. You love in me the very thing for which I am attacked. For why did I not embrace a mute and empty education? Why not one that is dry and drags downward? When I saw most people delighting in that, why did I utter strange and foreign wisdom and stand up against the opposing tongues? I should have run from argument with bold talk and called unreason faith, which I myself would have loved, as you well know, if I were a fisherman, since that is a ready excuse for ignorance among most people, if I had the power of miracles to serve in place of argument. May envy perish from among men, the extravagance of those who feel it and the poison of those who suffer it, the one passion that is both most unjust and most just: most unjust because it harasses everything good, most just because it consumes those who harbor it. I will not curse those who first praised me, for they did not know what their praises would lead to. If they had known, perhaps they would have added a little abuse to hold back envy.
notes: Source has OCR spacing breaks, as in θερ μοτέρων, ὠφε λήσομεν, πό θου, ἑαυ τῶν, αἰ δεῖσθαι and similar; gloss reads them as continuous words; no text invented.

problems.why: LXX Daniel 13 is the Protestant book Susanna; the allusion is Susanna 5.
problems.fix: “Lawlessness came forth from elders in Babylon who seemed to judge Israel” (Susanna 5).
problems.ruling: Source says κατὰ τὸν Δανιήλ; the elders passage is Susanna (Daniel 13 in Theodotion/Vulgate). Citing 'Daniel 13:5' is nonstandard; Susanna 5 is the correct reference, so a reader is misled.

problems.source_quote: οἳ ἐδόκουν κρί νειν τὸν Ἰσραήλ
problems.why: ἐδόκουν means they were thought to judge, not that they claimed the role.
problems.ruling: ἐδόκουν κρίνειν means 'seemed/were thought to judge' (Susanna 5 'who were reputed to govern'). 'Claimed to judge' shifts it to self-assertion, changing the meaning.

problems.quote: if only my speech had the power of miracles
problems.source_quote: εἰ λόγον εἶχον τῶν σημείων τὴν δύναμιν
problems.why: This is a condition: if the power of signs served as my argument. The English turns it into a wish about his speech.
problems.fix: if I had the power of miracles to serve in place of argument.
problems.ruling: εἰ λόγον εἶχον τὴν δύναμιν is a condition: if sign-power were his argument. “If only” plus inverted subject turns it into a wish.

edits.old: if only my speech had the power of miracles
edits.new: if I had the power of miracles to serve in place of argument

fixed: wrong_scripture: (Daniel 13:5) changed to (Susanna 5), since LXX Daniel 13 is Susanna and source is κατὰ τὸν Δανιὴλ.
mistranslation: who claimed to judge Israel changed to who seemed to judge Israel, since source οἳ ἐδόκουν κρίνειν means were reputed/seemed to judge.

modality: if only my speech had the power of miracles changed to conditional if I had the power of miracles to serve in place of argument, since source εἰ λόγον εἶχον τῶν σημείων τὴν δύναμιν makes signs stand in place of speech.

last_rejected.source_quote: τὴν πικρὰν καὶ ἄποτον Μερρὰν τῷ τῆς ζωῆς ξύλῳ κατεγλυκάναμεν
last_rejected.why: Bitterness is named at Exodus 15:23; the wood that sweetens Marah is 15:25.
last_rejected.fix: I have sweetened bitter, undrinkable Marah with the wood of life (Exodus 15:25).
last_rejected.ruling: Citation "(Exodus 15:23)" marks the Marah episode (Μερρὰν); 15:23–25 is one narrative, and a link at the Marah verse is within normal practice, so no meaning is misled.
